data.title: Sitno – a prehistoric hillfort of the Lusatian culture
data.excerpt: With an area of some 16 hectares, the hillfort on the summit of Sitno is the highest-lying fortified point of the Lusatian culture in Slovakia and perhaps in the whole of central Europe. Andrej Kmeť was the first to investigate it; later work by the Slovak Mining Museum and the Institute of Archaeology in Nitra yielded pottery, querns, a metalworking workshop and a bronze hoard found in 1986.

children.text: The archaeological site of Sitno was first investigated at the end of the 19th century by Andrej Kmeť. His work was later continued by staff of the Slovak Mining Museum in Banská Štiavnica (Ján Truchlík, Zora Liptáková and Jozef Labuda). In recent years, in connection with more extensive building activity, rescue excavation has been carried out here by the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra in cooperation with the Slovak Mining Museum.

The prehistoric hillfort occupies the summit area of Sitno; from the north, west and south it is naturally protected by steep andesite crags. The only possible access to this space fortified by nature is from the east. That is precisely why the people of the Lusatian culture built a massive rampart fortification here during the Final Bronze Age. An ideal defensive system was thus created, consisting partly of the natural protection of the rocky precipices and partly of artificial ramparts running in two lines. The first is formed by the outer circuit rampart, which joins the Sitno crags from the south and from the north; its task was to absorb the first onslaught of attackers. On the eastern side it is well preserved to this day; from the south it combines with the rocky precipices and can be seen only as a barely visible rise. The whole rampart was later, in the Middle Ages (probably in the 13th century), adapted into massive walls which, together with the medieval castle, formed a single fortified whole. The second line of the rampart fortification is formed by the transverse rampart, which divides the hillfort into a lower and an upper part (its remains are visible by the lower station of the ski lift). This rampart was not used for defensive purposes in the Middle Ages. The summit of Sitno can therefore, in a certain sense of the word, be called an acropolis, and it also contained an abundant spring of water.

children.text: The whole area of the hillfort covers approximately 16 hectares and is the highest-lying fortified point of the people of the Lusatian culture during the Final Bronze Age (1000 to 700 years BC) in Slovakia, and perhaps within central Europe as well.

During the excavation of the acropolis at the site of the transmitter building no archaeological features could be found, only a large quantity of pottery fragments of the Lusatian culture which bear clear traces of influence from the area of the Kyjatice culture (the south of central Slovakia) and of the Middle Danube Urnfield culture (the south of western Slovakia). The people living on Sitno in the Final Bronze Age thus lived on the border of these three great cultures. The pottery sherds were grouped in clusters, from which more closely undetermined settlement features, probably of a seasonal character, may be inferred. Besides pottery, clay spindle whorls used in spinning thread were found here, as well as stone querns together with grain rubbers, fragments of bronze jewellery such as torcs and pins, and a large number of stone and clay discs, probably of a cult character. The bronze objects, together with part of a stone mould for casting small bronze chisels found earlier, confirm the supposition that a metalworking workshop existed in this part of Sitno. Alongside these objects of the Final Bronze Age, medieval pottery and a Roman coin of the 2nd century AD were found in the area of the acropolis.

children.text: The space between the acropolis and the transverse rampart (the upper part of the hillfort) has been terraced in some places, but it shows only minimal signs of occupation. For the time being it is not possible to determine exactly what this space served for.

The space between the transverse and the circuit rampart (the lower part of the hillfort) was densely occupied both in prehistory and in the Middle Ages. The settlement features are concentrated close to both ramparts, the medieval ones following the terracing of the ground. The greatest concentration of occupation, however, lies close to the circuit rampart. Here, in a complicated stratigraphy of soil layers, further complicated by soil washed down from higher-lying places, countless pottery sherds of the Final Bronze Age came to light, analogous to those from the acropolis, along with dozens of stone querns and grain rubbers, clay spindle whorls and loom weights, stone and clay discs, fragments of bronze torcs and of bronze vessels (in the places where Kmeť once found a complete vessel), indeterminable bronze sheet fragments and a bronze arrowhead. A settlement feature of this period with a hearth was also found, and in its immediate vicinity a stone quern, a grain rubber, a spindle whorl and a fragment of a loom weight together with pottery, which shows that the whole find assemblage dates to the Final Bronze Age.

children.text: In 1986 an archaeological excavation was carried out at the site by Dr Pavel Žebrák of the Institute of Archaeology of the Slovak Academy of Sciences in Nitra. In a hiding place beneath the floor of a chalet he succeeded in discovering an important find of a bronze hoard in the form of a decorated belt, bracelets, torcs, temple rings, a pin, wire rings and an ornament in the shape of an hourglass.

Given the miniature size of the objects, we may assume that the find belonged as jewellery to a young girl, who may have been a member of the family of the tribal chieftain of Sitno. The Bronze Age hoard is on display in the archaeological exhibition of the Old Castle.

The medieval occupation is connected with the terracing of the ground. Settlement features of this period (roughly the 13th to the 16th century) can be traced on the terraces in the form of roughly square pits of varying size and depth. Around them there is plenty of medieval pottery, structural ironwork (nails, cramps and the like), iron horseshoes, keys, rod-type locks and knives decorated with false damascening. Close to the gateway, which has served its purpose in this place from prehistory down to the present day, a large quantity of iron slag was found, which testifies to medieval metalworking activity at the site. The relationship between the medieval occupation and the castle remains unclear for the time being.

children.text: Besides the occupation in the Final Bronze Age and in the High Middle Ages, traces of the Slavs were also identified (a rotary quern and several pottery sherds of the 2nd century BC). The Roman coin already mentioned belongs to the 2nd century AD.
